questions.prompt: What problem does Layla notice after Devon's first jump?

choices.A: Devon stepped beyond the takeoff line.
choices.B: The tape's zero mark had shifted into the sand.
choices.C: Another athlete's number was on the clipboard.
choices.D: The measuring tape had snapped.

questions.correctAnswer: The tape's zero mark had shifted into the sand.
questions.explanation: Layla sees that the tape no longer begins at the takeoff line.
questions.stimulusText:
Layla's job at the community track meet was to record long-jump distances. After every jump, she checked the measuring tape, called out the result, and wrote it beside the athlete's number.
During the final round, a jumper named Devon landed farther than anyone had all afternoon. The crowd cheered when another volunteer announced a meet record. Layla looked down to enter the number, but the tape's zero mark no longer touched the takeoff line. Its metal end had shifted several inches into the sand.
“We can straighten it for the next jump,” the volunteer whispered. “Everyone already heard the result.”
Layla studied the rake marks. The tape had been in the correct place before Devon jumped, but someone smoothing the pit afterward must have moved it before the measurement was read. She could not tell exactly how far Devon had traveled.
Layla raised her hand to stop the announcement. The cheering faded as she explained the problem. Devon's smile disappeared, yet he asked for another attempt rather than arguing.
Before the jump, Layla and Devon checked the zero mark together. His second distance was slightly shorter than the announced record, but it was still the day's best.
As Layla wrote the official result, Devon thanked her. She had expected him to be disappointed. Instead, he tapped the number on her clipboard and said, “Now I know that one is mine.”

questions.prompt: Where does drifting snow mainly settle after wind passes through a snow fence?

choices.A: Directly beneath the fence
choices.B: On the downwind side
choices.C: Only at the fence's outer edges
choices.D: On the upwind roadway

questions.correctAnswer: On the downwind side
questions.explanation: Slower air releases drifting snow mainly on the downwind side of the fence.
questions.stimulusText:
A snow fence is not designed to stop every snowflake like a solid wall. Instead, it changes the movement of wind. Most snow fences contain open spaces between boards or through mesh. As wind passes through those openings, it slows and becomes less able to carry drifting snow. The snow then settles mainly on the downwind side of the fence.
This effect can help keep snow from piling onto a road, railway, or building entrance. Placement is crucial. If a fence stands too close to the area being protected, the resulting drift may form exactly where it causes trouble. Designers estimate the likely length of the drift and position the fence far enough away.
Height and openness also matter. A taller fence can influence a larger area, while a completely solid barrier may create strong swirling air near its edges. The most effective design depends on typical wind direction, landscape, snowfall, and available space.
Snow fences may be made from wood, synthetic mesh, or even rows of shrubs. Living fences can serve additional purposes, such as providing habitat, but they take time to grow. Temporary fences can be moved as needs change. In every form, successful snow control depends on guiding wind and choosing a location based on observed conditions rather than simply placing a barrier beside the place that must remain clear.

questions.prompt: What evidence suggests that the tool had been used for soap?

choices.A: The brass tubes were completely smooth.
choices.B: A faint floral scent remained inside the wooden frame.
choices.C: The inventory sheet contained a drawing of candles.
choices.D: The tool was displayed beside a farmhouse photograph.

questions.correctAnswer: A faint floral scent remained inside the wooden frame.
questions.explanation: The passage specifically mentions the floral scent as evidence of soap use.
questions.stimulusText:
Luca was preparing a display for the school museum when he found two labels for the same brass tool. One card, written decades earlier, called it a candle mold. A newer inventory sheet described it as a device for shaping soap.
The display opened on Monday. Luca could have selected the newer label and discarded the older one, but the disagreement bothered him. He examined the tool again. Its narrow metal tubes could have held wax, yet a faint floral scent remained inside the wooden frame.
In the museum office, Luca found a notebook donated with the tool. The first pages described winter evenings when a family made candles for its farmhouse. Years later, the same family began producing small bars of scented soap to sell at a market. A sketch showed the brass tubes being lined with paper before the soap mixture was poured.
Luca replaced both labels with a longer card. It explained that the object had begun as a candle mold and was later adapted for soap. He placed copies of the two original descriptions beside the notebook sketch.
On opening day, visitors spent more time at the tool than at several larger objects. They debated which use seemed more surprising and studied the scratches that both activities had left. Luca had worried that conflicting labels would weaken the display. Instead, the corrected label revealed a story of change that a single description would have hidden.

questions.prompt: What allows water in a rain garden to soak downward gradually?

choices.A: Layers of soil and gravel
choices.B: A sealed concrete floor
choices.C: A roof built over the plants
choices.D: Pipes that pump water uphill

questions.correctAnswer: Layers of soil and gravel
questions.explanation: The second paragraph identifies layers of soil and gravel as helping the water move downward.
questions.stimulusText:
During a heavy rain, water runs from roofs, sidewalks, and parking lots into storm drains. This runoff can carry soil, oil, litter, and other materials toward streams. When a large amount of water reaches a drainage system at once, streets may also flood.
A rain garden is a shallow planted area designed to collect some of that runoff. It is often placed lower than the surrounding ground so water can flow into it. Layers of soil and gravel allow the water to soak downward gradually. Plant roots help keep the soil open and may trap some materials carried by the water.
The plants in a rain garden must tolerate changing conditions. After a storm, the garden may be temporarily wet. During dry weather, the same area may receive little water. Native grasses, flowers, and shrubs are often selected because they can survive local weather and provide food or shelter for insects and birds.
A rain garden is not intended to remain a pond. Designers consider how quickly the soil drains and avoid locations where water could threaten a building's foundation. Leaves and litter must be removed, and damaged plants may need replacement. With suitable placement and maintenance, a rain garden can reduce the speed and amount of runoff entering drains while adding green space to a neighborhood.

questions.stimulusText:
During a heavy rain, water runs from roofs, sidewalks, and parking lots into storm drains. This runoff can carry soil, oil, litter, and other materials toward streams. When a large amount of water reaches a drainage system at once, streets may also flood.
A rain garden is a shallow planted area designed to collect some of that runoff. It is often placed lower than the surrounding ground so water can flow into it. Layers of soil and gravel allow the water to soak downward gradually. Plant roots help keep the soil open and may trap some materials carried by the water.
The plants in a rain garden must tolerate changing conditions. After a storm, the garden may be temporarily wet. During dry weather, the same area may receive little water. Native grasses, flowers, and shrubs are often selected because they can survive local weather and provide food or shelter for insects and birds.
A rain garden is not intended to remain a pond. Designers consider how quickly the soil drains and avoid locations where water could threaten a building's foundation. Leaves and litter must be removed, and damaged plants may need replacement. With suitable placement and maintenance, a rain garden can reduce the speed and amount of runoff entering drains while adding green space to a neighborhood.

questions.stimulusText:
Nia's science-fair project compared three materials used to soften echoes. She lined identical cardboard booths with felt, cork, or folded paper, then played the same recorded tone inside each one. Her sound meter showed that the cork booth was quietest.
During the morning judging period, the numbers changed. Now the felt booth appeared to perform best. Nia checked the lining and replayed the tone, but the second result remained.
Her partner Owen pointed toward a ventilation fan that had started above their table. Its low hum was barely noticeable in the crowded room. Nia moved the meter closer to the fan, and the reading rose.
They could have reported the quieter measurements collected before the fair. Instead, Nia wrote “background sound not controlled” across the results page. She and Owen asked to use an empty classroom during lunch. There, they placed every booth the same distance from the meter and repeated each test four times. Cork again produced the lowest average reading, although the difference was smaller than their first data suggested.
When the judges returned, Nia began by describing the fan rather than the winning material. One judge asked whether discovering the interference had weakened the project.
Nia glanced at the crossed-out chart. “It weakened our first conclusion,” she said, “but it strengthened the way we tested it.”
The judge nodded and spent the remaining time examining their revised procedure.

questions.prompt: What creates marks on thermal paper inside the printer?

choices.A: Tiny heating elements
choices.B: A refillable ink ribbon
choices.C: Pressurized air
choices.D: Ultraviolet light

questions.correctAnswer: Tiny heating elements
questions.explanation: Heating elements touch selected points and trigger the color-forming reaction.
questions.stimulusText:
Many receipts are printed on thermal paper, which can create dark marks without liquid ink. The paper contains a coating with color-forming chemicals that remain mostly colorless at ordinary temperatures. Inside a thermal printer, tiny heating elements touch selected points as the paper moves past. Heat triggers a reaction in the coating, producing letters, numbers, and images.
Because the printer does not need ink cartridges or ribbons, its mechanism can be compact and require relatively little routine maintenance. It can also print quickly and quietly. These advantages make thermal printing useful for receipts, labels, and tickets.
The same sensitivity that allows the paper to form an image can also cause problems. Prolonged heat or strong sunlight may darken areas that were not originally printed. Oils, plasticizers, and some cleaning substances can damage the coating or make the image fade. Friction may create marks as well.
For this reason, an important thermal receipt should be stored away from heat, bright light, and reactive materials. Even with careful storage, the image may not last as long as ink on durable paper. A digital copy can preserve information that might later fade. Thermal paper is therefore convenient for fast, short-term records, but it is less suitable when a document must remain readable for many years.

questions.stimulusText:
Imani had prepared twelve questions for her first turn hosting the community radio program. Her guest, Mr. Dorsey, repaired clocks and had promised to explain how he began the work.
The red studio light came on. Imani welcomed listeners and asked her opening question. Mr. Dorsey leaned toward the microphone, but no words followed. Through the glass, the producer pointed urgently at the clock.
Imani glanced at her list. Every question seemed too large: Why had he chosen his career? What made a clock worth saving? She heard the quiet seconds stretching.
Then she noticed a tiny brass gear beside Mr. Dorsey's hand. “What clock did that come from?” she asked.
Mr. Dorsey looked down and smiled. The gear belonged to the first clock he had repaired, a kitchen clock that his grandmother refused to discard. As he described searching for the fault, he forgot to watch the studio light. Imani asked how he knew which part had failed, and the conversation began to flow.
Afterward, the producer praised Imani for filling the silence. She shook her head. “I stopped trying to fill it,” she said. “I looked for something he was ready to talk about.”
On her list, Imani crossed out three broad questions. Beside the others, she wrote a reminder: begin with what is present, then follow the answer.

questions.prompt: Which metals may serve as sacrificial anodes?

choices.A: Zinc, magnesium, or aluminum
choices.B: Iron, copper, or silver
choices.C: Steel, tin, or gold
choices.D: Lead, brass, or nickel

questions.correctAnswer: Zinc, magnesium, or aluminum
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists these reactive metals as possible sacrificial anodes.
questions.stimulusText:
When iron or steel is exposed to water and oxygen, chemical reactions can produce rust. Paint and other coatings slow corrosion by separating metal from its surroundings, but a scratch may leave the surface vulnerable. Another protection method uses a more reactive metal.
Zinc, magnesium, or aluminum can be electrically connected to the steel that must be protected. Because the attached metal reacts more readily, it corrodes first. It is often called a sacrificial anode because it is gradually consumed while helping preserve the steel.
This method is used on structures that are difficult to keep perfectly coated, including ship hulls, underground pipelines, and some water heaters. The protective metal must make good electrical contact with the steel, and the surrounding water or damp soil helps complete the electrochemical process.
A sacrificial anode does not last forever. Workers inspect it and replace it after too much material has been consumed. The amount and placement of protective metal must also suit the structure and environment. A small anode may be exhausted too quickly, while poor contact may prevent it from working effectively. The method succeeds not by stopping every chemical reaction, but by directing the more damaging corrosion away from an important structure and toward a replaceable material.

questions.stimulusText:
When iron or steel is exposed to water and oxygen, chemical reactions can produce rust. Paint and other coatings slow corrosion by separating metal from its surroundings, but a scratch may leave the surface vulnerable. Another protection method uses a more reactive metal.
Zinc, magnesium, or aluminum can be electrically connected to the steel that must be protected. Because the attached metal reacts more readily, it corrodes first. It is often called a sacrificial anode because it is gradually consumed while helping preserve the steel.
This method is used on structures that are difficult to keep perfectly coated, including ship hulls, underground pipelines, and some water heaters. The protective metal must make good electrical contact with the steel, and the surrounding water or damp soil helps complete the electrochemical process.
A sacrificial anode does not last forever. Workers inspect it and replace it after too much material has been consumed. The amount and placement of protective metal must also suit the structure and environment. A small anode may be exhausted too quickly, while poor contact may prevent it from working effectively. The method succeeds not by stopping every chemical reaction, but by directing the more damaging corrosion away from an important structure and toward a replaceable material.
